title: Put out into the deep (Novo Millennio Ineunte)
hookLine: John Paul II begins the millennium with duc in altum
tomorrow: why would a pope say faith doesn't start with a rule?

cards: Lap pools have a rope where the floor drops away. On one side your feet touch. On the other, they don't.
A fisherman named Simon is on the shallow side this morning. He's fished all night on the lake and caught nothing, and he's washing his nets on the shore.

A teacher steps into his boat, asks him to push off a little, and teaches the crowd from the water. Then he turns to Simon. In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught."
Simon is tired. He knows this lake. He knows the night is over.

teach.h: AT THY WORD I WILL LET DOWN THE NET.
teach.b: His answer is honest. Master, we worked all night and took nothing. But at your word, I'll let down the net.
He doesn't pretend the night went well. He goes anyway. And Luke says the nets fill until they start to break.

teach.h: A LETTER AS THE JUBILEE CLOSES.
teach.b: Centuries later, John Paul the Second wrote a letter as the Great Jubilee closed.
It's called Novo Millennio Ineunte, at the beginning of the new millennium, and he opens it with this scene, in Latin: duc in altum, put out into the deep. Here's the surprise.
A pope at a turning point might be expected to unveil a big new plan. He says the opposite. No formula will save us, he writes; a person will.
The program already exists: the Gospel, centered on Christ. So where's the deep water? He names it.
Holiness, which he calls the measure of ordinary Christian life, not a prize for a few.
And prayer: he asks parishes to become real schools of prayer. The deep isn't some far-off sea.
It's the same boat, the same lake, the same nets. Just farther from the shore, at someone else's word.

how: Readers of Novo Millennio Ineunte take its call to holiness and prayer into ordinary parish life, and some parishes and schools take duc in altum as a motto.

games.q: what does “put out into the deep” mean?
o: Jesus' words to Simon: row farther out and let down the nets
a rule telling monks to pray far away from the towns
advice to take on big risky projects alone, right away

games.q: put out into the deep — tap the pairs.
p: Latin: put out into the deep
at the beginning of the new millennium
what parishes are asked to become

s: duc in altum means taking big, risky leaps into something brand new
in John Paul's letter it means going deeper in the same Gospel: holiness and prayer.
Simon had fished all night and caught nothing before he rowed back out
Luke says so, and Simon goes anyway, at Jesus' word.
in the letter, holiness is meant for a few special people
John Paul calls it the measure of ordinary Christian life.

games.q: a friend has volunteered at the same food pantry for two years and says it's gone flat. what would duc in altum suggest?
o: quit and start something bigger somewhere new.
stay, and go one step deeper there: learn names, stay after.
keep it exactly the same and wait for the feeling to return.
games.why: John Paul's deep water is the same boat and the same nets, farther from shore. not a new program: the same work, lived deeper.

practice: Choose one part of your inner life that stays near the shore: prayer, scripture, the way you treat one person. Name one stroke farther out, name what usually stops you, and name one plain step for this week.
If you pray, you can hand him the empty nets first, the way Simon did.

wordCard.voice: Put out into the deep. Jesus to a tired fisherman in Luke, and John Paul the Second's word to the Church at a new millennium.

orig.note: Latin for put out into the deep: Luke 5:4 in the Vulgate, the words John Paul chose for the new millennium.

carryVoice: Your line: duc in altum. Same boat, same nets, a little farther from the shore. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught.

sources.ref: Luke 5:1–6 (the boat, the empty night, Simon's answer, the breaking nets)
